passage:
Thursday
Today Nitin came to me at the water cooler with his eyes all shiny. "Varun, did you hear about Kamala? Her mother shouted at her outside the gate, and she was crying, and..."
I just said, "I don't want to talk about it. It's her business." Nitin looked at me like I had grown two heads. "Fine, boring," he said and walked off.
My ears went hot. I thought maybe he would stop being my friend. But at lunch he sat with me anyway and we played book cricket.
I didn't tell anyone about Kamala. At least one person in class 5 didn't.
Varun

qa.q: Where did Nitin come to talk to Varun?
qa.a: Nitin came to him at the water cooler.

qa.q: What was Varun worried about after refusing to listen?
qa.a: Varun worried that Nitin might stop being a friend, which is why Varun's ears went hot.

qa.q: What does Varun's choice do to the story about Kamala?
qa.a: By not passing it on, Varun takes away one carrier, so the story has one less path to travel and may die out sooner.

qa.q: How might Kamala feel if she knew what Varun did?
qa.a: She would likely feel relieved and a little safer, knowing at least one classmate protected her privacy. 🙂

grounding: It shows a child refusing to listen to or repeat a rumour, saying it is the girl's own business, which shortens the story's life.

passage: The bus to the Tehsil school was late again, and the children waited under the peepal tree by the dhaba. Samir came running, out of breath. "Kunal! Listen! Shabnam's family had a fight with the sarpanch, and my cousin says they'll have to leave the village!" Two younger boys crowded close. Kunal kept his eyes on the road. "I don't want to hear it, Samir. That's her family's matter." Samir's grin slipped. "You're no fun." "Maybe," Kunal said. When the bus finally rattled up, the younger boys were already arguing about cricket instead. Nobody asked Samir to finish his story, and by the time they reached school, he had forgotten it too.

qa.a: They were waiting under the peepal tree by the dhaba.

qa.a: Kunal seemed uncomfortable with the gossip and wanted to show that Kunal did not want to be part of it, without making a big fight.

qa.a: Kunal calmly refusing to hear it worked, because without an interested listener the younger boys drifted to cricket and the story stopped there.

passage: In the small school near the paddy fields of Goa, Maria Miss closed the door after the prayer. "No lessons for ten minutes," she said. "I want to talk about words." She held up a crumpled sheet. "Once you crush paper, you can say sorry, but can you make it smooth again?" The class shook their heads. She did not say any name. But everyone knew about the story going around, and Dilnaz stared at her desk. After the bell, Maria Miss knelt by her. "If you want to talk, I'm here, or Sister Agnes in the office." At lunch, when someone whispered the story again, Dilnaz said clearly, "That isn't true." Her voice was steady, and the whisperer went quiet.

qa.q: What did Maria Miss hold up to the class?
qa.a: She held up a crumpled sheet of paper.

qa.q: How can you tell Dilnaz felt more confident by lunch?
qa.a: She said "That isn't true" clearly and with a steady voice, instead of staring at her desk like she did in the morning.

qa.q: What made Maria Miss's approach helpful?
qa.a: She talked about how words hurt without naming Dilnaz, so no one was embarrassed further, and then privately offered herself or Sister Agnes as someone to talk to.

qa.q: How might the whisperer see things after the class talk and Dilnaz's reply?
qa.a: They may feel caught and a little ashamed, realising the class now sees the story as hurtful and Dilnaz is not afraid of it.

grounding: It shows a teacher speaking to the class about hurtful words without naming the girl, offering her a trusted adult, and the girl calmly stating the truth.

passage: Outside the classroom window in Valencia, the orange trees swayed. Mr Santiago put down his marker. "Something has been going round this class," he said. "I'm not going to repeat it or say who it's about. But I want you to imagine hearing your name in a whisper, and not knowing what comes after it." Nobody spoke. Marek, the new boy, looked at his shoes. Later, as the class filed out, Mr Santiago quietly told Lucía, "The school counsellor, Ms Ortega, is very kind. Or you can talk to me anytime." Next morning, when a girl asked her in the corridor if the story was true, Lucía said, "No. It isn't." Just that. She walked on, and it felt better than hiding.

qa.q: What was swaying outside the classroom window?
qa.a: The orange trees were swaying outside the window.

qa.a: She felt stronger and relieved, because saying the truth simply felt better than hiding.

passage: The physics coaching class had already started when Mahima and Rishabh slipped in together, ten minutes late, both holding umbrellas. Deepak, in the back row, sat up straight. Together? Again? He remembered them laughing at the canteen last week. He didn't know that Mahima's scooter had broken down and Rishabh lived on the same road. By the time the teacher wrote the first formula, Deepak's mind had written a whole story. He could already picture telling the boys at the tea stall. He'd be the one who knew first. Nobody would call him the quiet one then. His fingers itched towards his phone. "Deepak, the answer?" the teacher asked. He hadn't even heard the question.

qa.a: He wanted to be the one who knew first and to feel important, so no one would call him the quiet one.

qa.q: What could Deepak do at this spark stage to stop a rumour before it starts?
qa.a: He could notice that he is only guessing, since arriving together has many ordinary reasons, and keep the idea to himself or simply ask them later.

qa.a: His exciting story would fall apart, and he would see that two neighbours sharing a ride is ordinary news, not gossip.

passage: In Chhindwara the power had gone off again, but everyone's phones still glowed. Darshan was on the rooftop with his phone, scrolling the class group. Someone had posted a blurry photo of Madhav and Leela sharing an umbrella near the bus stand. Darshan typed, "Umbrella couple!" with a laughing face. Within a minute there were twenty replies. Someone added that they held hands. Someone else said her father had seen them at the fair. Darshan felt the rush of it and wrote, "Wedding in March," and more laughing faces piled up. Then Leela's cousin posted, "She was just walking home, stop it." But by then the screenshots were already in three other groups, and the correction sat unread at the bottom.

passage: It was a grey afternoon in Gothenburg when Oskar posted in the year-nine chat: "Chen and Alva left the party early together 👀" with a laughing emoji. Mia replied with three laughing faces. Someone added that Alva had been crying. Someone else said Chen's jacket was in her locker. None of it had been checked. Oskar watched the numbers climb on his phone and added a joke about a wedding cake. It felt like a game. By evening, Chen messaged the group himself: "I walked her to the tram because she felt sick. passage:
Saturday night
The class chat has been going crazy about Aadhya since afternoon. The screenshot, the laughing faces, the comments. I read every message. I didn't laugh. I felt sick, actually.
I typed "guys this is not okay" three times and deleted it three times. Because I know how it works. The second you defend someone, you're the next joke. Last year it was Pratik, just for one comment.
So I just watched. Forty-two people in the group and only eight are posting. The rest of us are like me, I bet. Quiet.
But when nobody says anything, it looks like everybody agrees. And Aadhya is seeing all of it.
Yash

qa.a: Yash was afraid of becoming the next joke, like Pratik last year, if Yash defended Aadhya.

I'm Akash. Last term, when that edited picture of Jahnavi went round, she wanted to make a video and "destroy them all." I understood. I was angry too. But I'd seen what happened to another girl who replied in public: fifty new comments by morning.
So I did two things. I messaged the three boys who first shared it, one by one: "It's not true. Please delete it." Two did. One laughed, but at least he stopped posting.
Then I sat with Jahnavi outside the staff room until she was ready to knock on Mrs Kulkarni's door. I didn't do the talking. I just stayed.
